Since you seem committed, I'll tell you the secret that takes everyone years to learn. The goal of a bike race is **not** to go as fast as possible. It is to cross the line first. Those two things are not the same.

Your race is a criterium. There are many ways to win a criterium, none of which are easy:
-Solo away (simply ride faster than the other competitors combined)
-win the group sprint
-make a bold solo move with (x) to go (usually one lap to go)
-stay out of the wind for the entire race and get lucky somehow

Your method should depend on your strengths as a cyclist, which are probably the same as your strengths as a swimmer. If you were a sprint swimmer, then you could probably do a long sprint without a leadout and be okay. If you were a distance swimmer and you're willing to push yourself, you might have the endurance to go solo (but that also requires luck, courage, natural talent, and some extreme bike handling skills to corner effectively).

You may not win this criterium, but it's a good introduction to the sport. Read all you can, including:
http://303cycling.com/5-golden-rules-to-criterium-racing

Since you have a power meter, you should read The Cyclists Training Bible and Training and Racing With a Power Meter, both of which are about $15 online.

When someone mentions 'steroids', they could be referring to various substances. In common usage, it typically means *anabolic* steroids, which are muscle-building agents. These are the substances that athletes often get caught using. They are illegal and banned for numerous reasons. Frequently, users take doses that are 100-1000 times higher than clinical recommendations, leading to significant side effects. In severe cases, tendons can become so weak that they tear. This is a clear indicator in bodybuilding: if someone experiences a tendon rupture, they are likely using these substances. There are many other side effects, some of which are well-known: excessive body hair in women, breast development in men, reduced testicle size, and those are among the less severe effects, as they are not life-threatening. The risk of cancer is a serious concern with these drugs.

Now, if you're discussing steroids for anti-inflammatory purposes, the same principles apply. The steroids we use can range from corticosteroids (with cortisol being the most common) to inhaled steroids (like certain asthma medications). The short answer is that there are numerous side effects, including mood swings, acne, and bloating.

Another issue is that many individuals do not respond well to corticosteroids. A certain percentage may have allergies, and many conditions may not be related to inflammation. Roughly 30% of individuals who receive a cortisone injection (indicating they were appropriate candidates: their injury seemed likely to respond, it matched their treatment plan, and the healthcare provider chose to administer it) do not see any benefit.

In comparison, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) carry minimal risk. The primary side effect of ibuprofen is that prolonged use at clinical doses can lead to stomach ulcers. They are effective for about 90% of individuals, and they are inexpensive and easy to use. However, injuries related to cycling tend to be severe and chronic, often developing over time before a cyclist decides to address them, which means they can take a long time to heal. Additionally, cyclists are unlikely to stop cycling long enough for the injury to fully recover.

In all honesty, we should be more open to using cortisol in young, healthy cyclists. However, the healthcare providers available to most people may be hesitant due to the trade-offs involved. Sports medicine doctors associated with athletic teams are often more willing to prescribe cortisol to an athlete, as they prioritize immediate performance over long-term health.

In summary: There are many side effects. Healthcare providers prefer to try conservative treatments first.

Wall of text warning. Let me start by saying that I did everything *wrong* and then figured out how to do it right.

**0) Find out what you want to study.**
That sounds really easy. I promise it's not. I recommend a field in science, technology, engineering, or mathematics (STEM). Computer science is a really good idea. Business isn't a bad idea if you're not opposed to getting a graduate degree (expensive) and have strong interpersonal and leadership skills. Those can be refined, but they can't be taught. If you're numerically and scientifically inclined, engineering is probably the best way to go. It will be the most challenging four years of your life, but the rest of your life will be much easier if you do it right.

**1) Start out at a community college.**
The first two years of most majors will be pretty similar: basic English, basic history, philosophy, etc. They call these 'core' classes. My institution also referred to freshman and sophomore classes (100 and 200 level) as 'lower level'. Most state universities will accept an associate's degree, which community colleges offer, as completing all of your core lower division requirements. Watch out for science (e.g., engineering). Sometimes you take classes in the first two years that also count for your major; you would still have to take those (e.g., calculus 3).

Another awesome thing is that my community college offers 'guaranteed transfer' classes. These are usually things like what I mentioned above: introductory biology, English composition, introductory philosophy, etc. They are promised to transfer to the exact same course at a state university. So, Biology 111 at community college is worth Biology 1110 at the flagship state university.

Let me emphasize this point for a moment: One semester of tuition at my community college was $1400. One semester at my flagship state university was $5500. Frankly, I had a better experience at the community college because of how much smaller the classes were. Plus, since I was taking 200-level courses, the students were shockingly dedicated – my microbiology and pathophysiology courses had the most prepared students I ever studied with, and that includes graduate-level pre-med students.

**1.5) Plan your degree.**
My university offered something called a Degree Audit. I suggest you actually find a list of courses required for your major. For example, my university would break their requirements down into subsections and then you had to get a certain number of hours from each subsection. As you saw from the link, I can get my Written Communication credits from any of those courses. Turns out, I needed to take a specific course in scientific writing for my degree anyway. Therefore, if I'd taken an extended first-year writing and rhetoric course, I would still have to take the scientific writing course, regardless. Therefore, be smart about what classes you can take. If you spend an extra 6-8 hours a semester planning your courses, you can save yourself a semester or two (at $5000 a semester, that’s a pretty good hourly rate) and get a great schedule (community college: All classes Tuesday / Thursday. It was a 10-hour day, but I had 5 days a week off).

**2) Apply for scholarships and financial aid.**
You must apply for financial aid to receive federal loans. You’re likely to get limited assistance, since you said that your family is in the picture. Financial aid assumes everyone lives in a nice neighborhood and your family will contribute a significant portion of their annual income to your schooling. Unfortunately, I’ve personally experienced that isn’t the case. So plan on receiving little to no federal aid. You won’t be considered independent for financial aid purposes until you’re 24, married, or meet a couple of other hard-to-find exemptions.

The next best thing, of course, is to apply for scholarships. I am a white male from an upper middle-class family, so I certainly had limited options. Still, I got two scholarships ($1,000 / yr for one paper, because no one else applied) and $750 / yr for books. Wasn’t a lot, and I eventually lost the big one because I made some mistakes, but hey, it saved me $3,000. Scholarships don’t just come from your school – they can also come from your community and local organizations.

Note on student loans: they aren’t the end of the world. Subsidized student loans are at a low interest rate in some cases. That’s a phenomenal rate. Other loans are at a moderate rate; that’s decent. But if you take out more than a specific amount, which hopefully you won’t need to, they will be at a higher interest rate. That’s not a great rate. If you can work and still take classes, it will minimize your cost of living.

**3) Work in a lab / gain experience.**
Look for entry-level positions in your field of choice. What do you find? Well, the salary might not be great, and people STILL want you to have 1-3 years' experience in your field. Hi there. Not a lawyer, but I worked at a physical therapy clinic similar to a well-known chain (including a combined doctor's office and physical therapy clinic).

Worker's comp is *not* private insurance, so the rules are a little different. The insurance company directs quite a bit of the care, and your state's laws determine what is or is not allowable.

It sounds like they are following the process as I know it:

* You get injured and report it to your employer
* Your employer opens a claim with the insurance
* You seek whatever emergency treatment you may need (in this case, going to the emergency room is OK)
* Afterward, they will send you to a worker's comp doctor (the clinic in question) to manage your care
* For an injury like this, they will send you to a specialist who will then direct your care (this will be an orthopedist, also called an orthopedic surgeon).

It appears this is where you stand. Up to this point, it sounds like they have followed the rules. That said, if you're unhappy with your care, you can work with your adjuster to switch to a different company. The adjuster is your contact with the insurance company. Become friends with this person, as they can be the difference between a good recovery and a bad recovery. Them seeing you as a person rather than just a file will very much help you get approved for more treatment.

In my state, insurance companies were allowed to recommend physical therapy before more radical (i.e., expensive) methods. This is absurd, but it's what my state laws allowed. For example, we had someone come in with a full thickness rotator cuff tear and the insurance declined surgery until we tried conservative treatment. Uh, the rope is torn in half. It's not going to heal with time.

That said: buckle in. There's a lot of nonsense in this process but it will get you recovered if you follow the rules and work hard. Form a relationship with your doctor. It sounds like you don't like the one you got; ask around and see who is a better worker's comp doctor who will help you get better.

Ultimately, the doctor will provide a medical opinion. Insurance can fight that, but they can't straight up ignore it. Find a doctor invested in your care.

If your situation is bad enough, you may be assigned a Nurse Case Manager. This is a person you *very* much want on your side. They ensure that complicated courses of treatment don't slip through the cracks. That person works for insurance, but they are nurses and generally very good at advocating for you.

The 'resetting the clock' is actually two concepts: there is the amount of time it can be on your report, and the amount of time you can be sued for it. Those are two different things.

**Claiming** the debt, which can be done by offering to pay the debt, paying any portion of the debt, setting up a payment plan, or even just acknowledging that "yes, the debt is valid," will all reset your Statute of Limitations. This is the amount of time you can be sued for it.

So TL;DR: keep trying to negotiate a pay-for-delete. Some companies won't accept them on principle. Either way, they will be off of your report after 7.5 years.

I worked in workers' compensation (in a region that statistically isn't yours).

Generally, you provide written notice within a certain number of days (my region is 48 hours / 2 days). That's pretty easy to get out of; explain that you spoke to your supervisor and they weren't helpful (true).

If you're going to be out of work for a month, I would *absolutely* file a claim. In fact, I'd file the claim even if I wasn't out of work. Your treatment will be FREE and covered 100% by insurance.

Generally, the process:

1) You speak to your supervisor (usually giving them written notice: "Hello supervisor & HR, please consider this notice that I had a work-related injury on 6/17/2017. I tripped in a hole and hurt my ankle on the job site while working. Signed, [your identifier]."

2) They work with your workers' compensation insurance. They open a claim, you get a claim number, and you go to the doctor. Your employer can tell you where they *recommend*, but they are required (in my region) to have 3+ different providers. If anyone asks why you waited so long, you can tell them that you wanted to see if it would heal before you made a big deal of it. That's true, that's factual, and it doesn't degrade your injury claim at all.

3) When you go to the doctor, don't expect a ton. This will be very basic: they'll give you some crutches and possibly some ibuprofen. The important thing is the workers' comp doctor will give you instructions on what your employer must do to help your recovery. This could be light duty; if the employer doesn't provide light duty, they *can* send you home. If that happens (in my region) you get 66% of your normal wages until you can do regular work again.

4) The workers' comp doctor may also send you to a specialist or order imaging: x-rays / MRI. In my clinic, we could have that turned around in 2 hours, but took 2-3 days if no emergency (as a non-medical professional, I would say your injury is non-emergency because it's been four days and you are already off work).

5) You follow these orders. If they tell you to see a specialist, go see them. They may also order imaging. They will make reports and referrals to your workers' comp doctor. Your employer must also follow orders: if you say "My doctor says I need to be on restricted duty," and they say "Too bad, you're loading trucks today," they will get into trouble for that.

6) Work closely with your insurance adjuster. This person is interesting: their job is to keep your injury as cheap as possible, but they are usually pretty smart and can be friendly. Be friends with them, treat them well, and work with them. They can make your life MUCH easier.

7) Take it as it comes. You *cannot* be fired for filing the claim, but you *can* be fired for not being able to work due to the injury. So if they're going to fire you, they'll fire you regardless of whether you open a claim or not.

TL;DR: You got injured at work. Have workers' comp pay for it. If they fire you for it, they still have to pay your claim, but at least you'll get free medical treatment and 66% wages until you can work again.

"Building credit" is not hard. Get a credit card and then pay it on time, in full, every month. Rinse, wash, repeat.

If you truly have no credit, getting the card is the hard part. You have three options:

* Have a partner add you as an authorized user on one of their cards. This card will now report to your credit as well. You don't need to use it (it can sit in a sock drawer) but anything that reports to their card will also report to yours: age of accounts, balances, utilization, etc. After this reports for a few months, request your own credit card since you now have credit history.

* Have a partner cosign on your credit card. Apply for a card and add them as a cosigner. They're legally agreeing to pay the card if you don't, including all the penalties if you don't. It's as much their debt as yours.

* If neither of those are options, you can get a student (if you are a student) or secured card. Student cards are preferred because you don't need to put money down, but you may not qualify. A secured card is when you put down a $200 security deposit for a $200 line of credit. You get that money back when you close the card (or, preferably, roll it into an unsecured card). Good options are secured cards from well-known financial institutions, because they have no annual fee so you can leave them open for a long time.

Get a card with no annual fee. Spend some time on credit comparison websites reading up on which card to get (keep in mind these sites may earn money by promoting certain products). You want an entry-level, barebones card.

All credit cards build credit at the same rate, and you don't qualify for anything with perks yet. If you go with options 1 or 2, consider mid-tier cards with great rewards (cashback) that are just really solid.

Finally: everyone worries about credit cards because they abuse them. Treat them like cash: understand that you should pay them off in full at the end of every month. If you do that, you don't pay interest (credit cards usually have high interest rates!) which means you pay about 1.8% on the total *per month* if you don't pay it off at the end of your billing period. So, just pay it off in full! That's 'responsible' use that everyone talks about.
